questions.question: Students often swap 'independent' and 'mutually exclusive'. Give one example of each and state the formula test that separates them.
questions.solution: Mutually exclusive: cannot co-occur — P(A∩B) = 0 (head and tail on one coin). Independent: one's occurrence doesn't change the other's probability — P(A∩B) = P(A)P(B) (two different coins). The tests differ: exclusive events with positive probabilities are NEVER independent (if A happened, B certainly didn't — dependence). Zero intersection vs product of probabilities is the discriminator.

questions.question: Why does P(A|B) use B as the new sample space, and why is P(A|B) ≠ P(B|A) in general?
questions.solution: Conditioning on B means 'given that B happened', so all probabilities are computed within B — P(A|B) = P(A∩B)/P(B), a re-weighting of the part of A inside B. P(A|B) ≠ P(B|A) because the denominators differ (P(B) vs P(A)): knowing a card is a king (P(heart|king) = ¼) differs from knowing it's a heart (P(king|heart) = 1/13).

questions.question: A test is 99% accurate for a disease affecting 1 in 1000. Why is a positive result NOT 99% likely to mean disease? Set up the Bayes computation.
questions.solution: P(D|+) = P(+|D)P(D) / [P(+|D)P(D) + P(+|¬D)P(¬D)] = (0.99×0.001)/(0.99×0.001 + 0.01×0.999) ≈ 0.09 — about 9%. The false positives from the huge healthy population (999×0.01 ≈ 10) swamp the true positives (1×0.99 ≈ 1). Base rate dominates: rare disease + imperfect test = mostly false alarms. This is the classic base-rate fallacy.

questions.question: State the four conditions for a binomial distribution B(n, p), and explain why 'number of heads in 10 flips' qualifies but 'number of sixes until the first head' does not.
questions.solution: Conditions: fixed number n of trials; each trial has two outcomes (success/failure); constant probability p per trial; trials independent. Heads in 10 flips satisfies all four. 'Sixes until first head' has an UNFIXED number of trials (a random stopping time) — it is a geometric-type situation, not binomial. Fixed n is the condition that fails.

questions.question: For B(n, p), show why mean = np is intuitive, and explain why the variance np(1−p) is largest at p = ½.
questions.solution: Each trial contributes p to the expected count (linearity of expectation over n identical trials) — mean np. Variance per trial is p(1−p): zero at p = 0 or 1 (outcome is certain, no spread) and maximal at p = ½ (maximum uncertainty). Uncertainty peaks where both outcomes are equally likely — the bell curve is widest there.

questions.concept: At least one — the complement trick
questions.question: Why is 'P(at least one success in n trials)' computed as 1 − (1−p)ⁿ rather than by adding n probabilities?
questions.solution: 'At least one' is the complement of 'none': P(≥1) = 1 − P(0) = 1 − (1−p)ⁿ. Adding the n separate 'exactly k' terms would work but is far longer. The complement collapses a union of many events into a single term — the standard trick whenever an event is described by 'at least'.

questions.concept: Random variable — the expectation as a weighted mean
questions.question: Why is E(X) = Σxᵢpᵢ called a weighted mean, and why can E(X) be a value X never takes (e.g. 3.5 for a die)?
questions.solution: E(X) weights each outcome by its probability — the centre of mass of the distribution. It need not be an ATTAINABLE value: a fair die's expectation is (1+2+…+6)/6 = 3.5, the balance point, though no single roll gives 3.5. Expectation describes the long-run average over many trials, not a single observation.

questions.question: Drawing 3 cards from a deck without replacement, why does the probability of 'exactly 2 aces' NOT follow the binomial formula?
questions.solution: Without replacement the trials are DEPENDENT: after an ace is drawn, p for the next trial changes (4/52 → 3/51). The binomial requires CONSTANT p and independence — both violated. Use the hypergeometric-style counting instead: C(4,2)·C(48,1)/C(52,3). Sampling without replacement is the standard binomial-breaker.
